{"answer": "# Classification of Aluminium Alloy Powder for LPBF: Achieving a 15–25 µm Lower Cut in a University Laboratory

## 1. Context and the Core Challenge

The AMAZEMET rePOWDER ultrasonic atomizer operating at approximately 40 kHz produces highly spherical aluminium alloy powders with a relatively narrow particle size distribution (PSD). Published data on similar systems report number-based D50 values of approximately 40–50 µm and volume-based D50 values of approximately 50–100 µm, with the majority of the powder below 100 µm (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000034). The standard PBF-LB/M-relevant fraction is 20–63 µm, as used in multiple published studies (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000041). LPBF suppliers typically provide aluminium-alloy powders in the 15–45 µm range (pqac-00000017). Achieving a lower cut at 15–25 µm from 200–500 g lots is the central challenge, because dry sieving methods become deficient below 45 µm (pqac-00000015).

## 2. Fine Woven-Wire Test Sieves (No. 635 / 20 µm and No. 450 / 32 µm) on a Mechanical Shaker

### Charge Limits, Throughput, and Standards

Per the Handbook of Non-Ferrous Metal Powders, the standard sieve analysis procedure (ISO 4497, ASTM B 214) uses a powder charge of 100–300 g on a sieve stack placed on a shaker with rotary and tapping action, sieving for 15–20 min (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000015). DIN 66165 Part 2 and ISO 2591-1 specify similar procedures for analytical test sieving and describe endpoint criteria based on mass change per unit time (typically <0.2% of the initial charge passing in an additional minute of sieving).

ASTM B 214 does not endorse hand sieving as an equivalent method. DIN 66165 similarly requires controlled mechanical agitation with defined amplitude and frequency. In published AM-powder preparation, AA2017 powder was mechanically sieved for 30 min using a vibrator with sieves from 20 to 250 µm (pqac-00000036); AlSi7Mg0.6 powder was sieved after each LPBF build cycle using standardized procedures (pqac-00000021).

### Hand Sieving Limitations

Hand sieving at 63 µm is marginally acceptable for spherical powder whose median is well above 63 µm, since most particles easily fall through. However, with the described Al-Si powder (smallest particles mostly 40–60 µm, median roughly 40–50 µm), the 45 µm sieve performs a near-median cut where sieving completeness is most sensitive to agitation intensity and duration. Hand sieving cannot provide the reproducible rotary-plus-tapping motion needed, resulting in:
- Poor completeness: 10–30% of near-mesh particles may be retained that should pass
- No objective endpoint criterion
- Uneven charge distribution and inconsistent particle reorientation
- Lower recovery and higher variability between operators

### Recommendation

**A mechanical sieve shaker is essential**, at minimum for the 45 µm sieve, and strongly recommended for any standardized operation at 63 µm. A Ro-Tap type (rotary + tapping, per ASTM B 214) is the standard for metal powders. Vibratory 3D shakers (e.g., Retsch AS 200) are also effective and widely used in AM-powder studies. For a university lab with 200 mm sieves, a compact vibratory shaker handling 1–3 sieves would be sufficient, at a cost of approximately $3,000–8,000.

## 8. Aluminium Dust Safety for All Options

### Explosion Characteristics

Aluminium dust is among the most hazardous combustible dusts. Key parameters for fine Al powder in the relevant 15–50 µm range (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000005):
- **Dust explosion class: St 3** (most severe)
- **Kst: 300–415+ bar·m/s** (depending on particle size and morphology)
- **Pmax: 10–12+ bar**
- **MIE: 3–10 mJ** (comparable to a static-electricity spark from a person)
- **MEC: approximately 30–60 g/m³** (a thin haze, easily achieved during pouring or sieving)
- **LOC: 10–12%** (requires robust inerting)

### Safety Requirements for Each Option

- **Dry sieving (test sieves or shaker):** Ground all equipment, the shaker, sieve frames, and the operator (conductive footwear, wrist strap). Use an enclosed sieve stack with a lid and receiver. Avoid vigorous open-air transfers. Work in a well-ventilated area or fume hood. Clean up all spills immediately (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000006).

- **Wet sieving:** Eliminates airborne-dust and static risks but introduces solvent-flammability and Al–water reactivity hazards. Never use water with Al powder. IPA or ethanol are flammable; ventilation and spark-free environments are essential (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000027).

- **Air-jet sieve:** The integral vacuum system is a major concern. Standard vacuum cleaners have brush motors (sparking) and non-conductive plastic components. An Al-rated collection system with conductive grounded components is required. The fines fraction is concentrated in the vacuum stream (pqac-00000004).

- **Air classifier:** Must operate in inert gas (N₂ or Ar) at O₂ below LOC (~10%). Collection cyclone and filter must be ATEX-rated. Grounding of all components is mandatory (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000004).

- **General lab handling per NFPA 484 / NFPA 652:** Housekeeping to prevent dust accumulation > 1/32 in (0.8 mm); bonding and grounding of all conductive equipment and containers; no open ignition sources; local exhaust ventilation at dust-release points; conductive containers for powder storage and transfer; moisture control to avoid H₂ generation from water-reactive metals (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000009).

## 10. Recommendation for a Lab Making 100–250 g per Run

### Primary Recommendation: Relax the Lower Cut to 20 µm and Use a Two-Stage Approach

Given the constraints (100–250 g per atomization run, no glovebox, 200 mm sieves, university budget), the most realistic approach is:

**Stage 1 — Upper cut with a mechanical sieve shaker (essential purchase):** Acquire a compact vibratory or tapping shaker for 200 mm sieves. Use the 63 µm and 45 µm sieves on the shaker with 100–200 g charges and 15–30 min cycles, per ISO 4497 / ASTM B 214 (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000015). This reliably produces the upper cut at 45 or 63 µm. For 200–500 g lots, run 1–3 passes. This is the minimum necessary investment and addresses the question of whether a shaker is needed: **yes, unequivocally.**

**Stage 2 — Lower cut:** The 15–25 µm lower cut is the difficult part. Given the SEM evidence that the smallest particles from the rePOWDER are mostly 40–60 µm, the fraction below 20 µm is likely very small (<2–5% by volume, based on the nickel-aluminium bronze data provided). Therefore:

- **If the sub-20 µm fraction is negligible (<2% by volume as measured by laser diffraction):** A lower cut may not be necessary. Simply use the 45 µm or 63 µm upper sieve and accept the full fines content for initial LPBF trials. Measure the PSD by laser diffraction to confirm.

Expect throughput of approximately 50–150 g/h and losses of 2–5%.

- **For a true 15–20 µm cut:** This requires access to an **air classifier (Hosokawa Alpine 50 ATP or equivalent) operating under inert gas**. This is best arranged through collaboration with a university or research institute that has such equipment, rather than purchasing one (cost >€50,000, plus ATEX compliance). Alternatively, toll classification can be attempted if lots of 2–5 kg can be accumulated. The documented approach of Cui et al. (2023), who used an Alpine 50 ATP to remove <20 µm fines followed by 63 µm sieving (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000037), is the closest published workflow to what this lab needs.

### What Not to Do

- **Do not wet-sieve Al powder in water:** Hydrogen evolution and severe oxidation render the powder unsuitable for LPBF (pqac-00000027).
- **Do not use a standard vacuum cleaner with an air-jet sieve for Al powder:** This is an explosion risk (pqac-00000004).
- **Do not rely on hand sieving at 45 µm:** It is unreproducible and standards-noncompliant for near-median cuts (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000015).

### Practical Starting Point

For immediate use: purchase a sieve shaker (~$3,000–8,000), stack the 250 µm / 63 µm / 45 µm sieves, process the 100–250 g rePOWDER output in a single shaker cycle (15–20 min), collect the −45 µm fraction, and measure its PSD by laser diffraction. If the sub-20 µm content is <2–3%, proceed to LPBF trials with the 20–45 µm window. If further classification is needed, add a 25 or 32 µm sieve and reduce the charge per pass. Ground all equipment, work in a ventilated area, and follow NFPA 484 dust-handling precautions throughout."}

# Classification of Aluminium Alloy Powder for LPBF: Achieving a 15–25 µm Lower Cut in a University Laboratory

## 1. Context and the Core Challenge

The AMAZEMET rePOWDER ultrasonic atomizer operating at approximately 40 kHz produces highly spherical aluminium alloy powders with a relatively narrow particle size distribution (PSD). Published data on similar systems report number-based D50 values of approximately 40–50 µm and volume-based D50 values of approximately 50–100 µm, with the majority of the powder below 100 µm (ciftcli2025alloydevelopmentfrom pages 3-6, zach2023sphericalpowderscontrol pages 1-2). The standard PBF-LB/M-relevant fraction is 20–63 µm, as used in multiple published studies (pennacchio2026effectofprocess pages 92-97, cui2023gasatomizationof pages 2-4, cui2023gasatomizationof pages 4-5). LPBF suppliers typically provide aluminium-alloy powders in the 15–45 µm range (munizlerma2018acomprehensiveapproach pages 1-3). Achieving a lower cut at 15–25 µm from 200–500 g lots is the central challenge, because dry sieving methods become deficient below 45 µm (neikov2019powdercharacterizationand pages 3-4).

## 2. Fine Woven-Wire Test Sieves (No. 635 / 20 µm and No. 450 / 32 µm) on a Mechanical Shaker

### Charge Limits, Throughput, and Standards

Per the Handbook of Non-Ferrous Metal Powders, the standard sieve analysis procedure (ISO 4497, ASTM B 214) uses a powder charge of 100–300 g on a sieve stack placed on a shaker with rotary and tapping action, sieving for 15–20 min (neikov2019powdercharacterizationand pages 3-4). DIN 66165 Part 2 and ISO 2591-1 specify similar procedures for analytical test sieving and describe endpoint criteria based on mass change per unit time (typically <0.2% of the initial charge passing in an additional minute of sieving).

For 200 mm (8 in) sieves at 20 or 32 µm, the recommended analytical charge per fine sieve is typically 25–75 g, well below the maximum for coarser meshes, to prevent overloading and blinding.

### Blinding and Sieving Aids

At apertures below 45 µm, dry sieving becomes "deficient" regardless of sieve type (neikov2019powdercharacterizationand pages 3-4). The main problems are: (a) overloading causes near-mesh particles to wedge into openings; (b) electrostatic charges cause fine particles to adhere to each other and to larger particles, forming agglomerates; and (c) irregularly shaped particles may pass only in certain orientations (neikov2019powdercharacterizationand pages 3-4). Recommended aids include commercial antistatic agents, rubber sieving balls or cubes to provide percussion and clearing action, and ultrasonic washing with a wetting agent if brushing fails to clear embedded particles (neikov2019powdercharacterizationand pages 3-4). Micromesh sieves (photo-etched electroformed nickel, per ASTM E 11-87, with ±2 µm tolerance from 125 to 5 µm) can be used on an air-jet sieve to extend the operational range down to approximately 10 µm (neikov2019powdercharacterizationand pages 3-4).

### Practical Assessment for 15–25 µm

A 20 µm woven-wire sieve on a tapping shaker would experience severe blinding from the Al-Si powder's 40–60 µm median fraction, with near-size particles rapidly plugging the mesh. A 32 µm sieve is marginal. For a 200–500 g batch, multiple passes at reduced charge (25–75 g per pass) with interim cleaning would be needed, giving a throughput of roughly 50–200 g/h. Sieve damage and shortened mesh life are significant concerns at these fine apertures, as damaged mesh openings distort and can stretch (neikov2019powdercharacterizationand pages 3-4).

## 3. Wet Sieving of Aluminium Powder

### Oxidation and Hydrogen Evolution

Aluminium reacts with water, evolving hydrogen gas and forming aluminium hydroxide. Published chemical surface treatment of AA2017 powder with NaOH and water documented hydrogen evolution and dramatic oxygen increases from 0.166 wt% in gas-atomized powder to approximately 3.65–3.69 wt% after aqueous treatment (batistao2026surfacefunctionalizationof pages 85-90). Drying subsequently converts hydroxide to oxide, permanently altering the surface chemistry.

### Solvent Choice

For aluminium sedimentation analysis, the Handbook of Non-Ferrous Metal Powders lists water (pH 3–4), cyclohexanol, cyclohexanone, isopropanol, and vegetable oil as suitable suspension liquids, with sodium tartrate (0.1 wt%) as dispersant (neikov2019powdercharacterizationand pages 4-6). For wet sieving, isopropanol or ethanol would avoid the hydrogen-evolution risk of water.

### Drying and Oxygen Pickup

Vacuum drying at 80 °C for 48 h has been used after wet treatment of Al powder (batistao2026surfacefunctionalizationof pages 69-73). Even controlled drying can accelerate oxide-layer growth: one study showed that furnace or vacuum drying of AlSi10Mg powder caused oxide thickness to increase from approximately 4 nm to 38 nm over reuse cycles, while bulk oxygen content rose from 500 ppm to 1250 ppm (lopes2026recyclabilityinmetal pages 9-11). Post-drying agglomeration can cause significant additional losses; after resieving, reported overall yields were only 69–78% (batistao2026surfacefunctionalizationof pages 69-73).

### LPBF Printing of Wet-Sieved Al

No published study was identified in which conventionally wet-sieved aluminium alloy powder was subsequently used for LPBF printing. The oxidation risk makes this approach unsuitable for producing qualified LPBF feedstock without rigorous oxygen analysis and process validation.

## 4. Air-Jet Sieves and Sonic Sifters

### Air-Jet Sieve (Hosokawa Alpine e200 LS)

The Alpine air-jet sieve uses a vacuum exhaust coupled with a rotating blowback nozzle that redistributes powder and disintegrates agglomerates, permitting sieving down to approximately 10 µm (neikov2019powdercharacterizationand pages 3-4). The Alpine 200LS-N has been used in pharmaceutical and food-science PSD analysis for fine fractions below 50 µm (as documented in granule-size analysis studies). Standard analytical sample mass is approximately 10–50 g per run, with a typical 3–10 min cycle. For preparative separation of 200–500 g, 10–50 repetitive cycles would be required, making this instrument impractical for routine production but valuable for verifying a cut or processing small development samples.

**Critically for aluminium dust safety,** the air-jet sieve's vacuum system presents a significant hazard. The vacuum cleaner motor, filter, and collection container must be rated for combustible metal dust. Standard laboratory vacuum cleaners are ignition sources. Grounding of all components and use of conductive collection vessels are mandatory.

### Sonic Sifter (ATM/Advantech L3P)

The sonic sifter uses oscillating air columns and mechanical pulses rather than continuous airflow. Its analytical capacity is typically 5–20 g per run. For 200–500 g, it would require dozens of cycles. The equipment can achieve cuts down to approximately 20 µm with appropriate meshes, but it is fundamentally an analytical instrument.

## 5. Benchtop Air Classifiers

### Published AM-Powder Classification Examples

Air classification is the technically preferred method for sharp fine cuts. Two key documented examples from the powder-bed-fusion literature:

- **Cui et al. (2023)** used a **Hosokawa Alpine Multiprocess 50 ATP** to remove fine particles below approximately 20 µm from gas-atomized duplex stainless steel powder, followed by mechanical sieving at 63 µm to produce a 20–63 µm PBF-LB/M fraction (cui2023gasatomizationof pages 2-4).

- **Spurek et al. (2021)** used a **Hosokawa Alpine air classifier** together with ultrasonic sieves to produce six monomodal 316L powder distributions with D50 values ranging from 10 to 60 µm and narrow widths of approximately 15 µm (D90–D10), specifically for PBF research (spurek2022influenceofthe pages 2-4, spurek2022influenceofthe pages 1-2).

### Operational Parameters

The Hosokawa Alpine 50 ATP / 100 MZR class systems can classify from approximately 2 to 100 µm. Once stabilized, throughput can reach several kg/h for typical powders. However, for 200–500 g batches, set-up, purging, and cleaning dominate the process time, and equipment hold-up losses (feeder, classifier rotor, cyclone, filter) can consume 5–20% or more of a sub-kilogram lot. This makes them best suited for batches exceeding approximately 1 kg.

### Inert-Gas Operation and ATEX/NFPA Compliance

Nitrogen or argon closed-loop operation is available on Hosokawa Alpine systems and is **mandatory** for aluminium powder classification. Aluminium dust in the relevant size range is classified as **St 3 (highly explosive)**: with a 29 µm mass-median diameter, it exhibits a minimum explosible concentration (MEC) of approximately 30 g/m³, maximum explosion pressure (Pmax) of 12.4 bar, and Kst of 415 bar·m/s (sezerUnknownyearalümi̇nyumtozpatlamalarinin pages 212-216). Fine aluminium powders have extremely low minimum ignition energies (MIE) of 3–4 mJ, making electrostatic discharge a credible ignition source (sezerUnknownyearalümi̇nyumtozpatlamalarinin pages 208-212). The limiting oxygen concentration (LOC) is approximately 10–12% (sezerUnknownyearalümi̇nyumtozpatlamalarinin pages 208-212). Any air classifier processing aluminium must be ATEX Zone 20 or NFPA 484 compliant, with all components grounded, inerted below LOC, and equipped with explosion-proof collection systems.

## 6. Toll Classification of Small Lots

Commercial toll classifiers (Hosokawa Alpine, AVEKA, Elcan Industries, Tekna) typically require minimum lots of 5–50 kg. A 200–500 g lot is far below any standard commercial minimum. Equipment hold-up alone on a pilot classifier may consume 50–200 g. The primary barrier is not technical capability but economic: setup, cleaning, qualification, and documentation costs are disproportionate to the lot size. A toll provider would need a micro-pilot or bench-scale classifier and a written mass-balance/recovery commitment for such small quantities.

## 7. Hand Sieving vs. Mechanical Shaker at 45 and 63 µm

### Standards Requirements

The standard sieve analysis procedures for metal powders (ISO 4497, ASTM B 214, MPIF Standard 05) specify a **mechanical shaker with rotary and tapping action** (neikov2019powdercharacterizationand pages 3-4). ASTM B 214 does not endorse hand sieving as an equivalent method. DIN 66165 similarly requires controlled mechanical agitation with defined amplitude and frequency. In published AM-powder preparation, AA2017 powder was mechanically sieved for 30 min using a vibrator with sieves from 20 to 250 µm (batistao2026surfacefunctionalizationof pages 69-73); AlSi7Mg0.6 powder was sieved after each LPBF build cycle using standardized procedures (smolina2022influenceofthe pages 6-8).

### Hand Sieving Limitations

Hand sieving at 63 µm is marginally acceptable for spherical powder whose median is well above 63 µm, since most particles easily fall through. However, with the described Al-Si powder (smallest particles mostly 40–60 µm, median roughly 40–50 µm), the 45 µm sieve performs a near-median cut where sieving completeness is most sensitive to agitation intensity and duration. Hand sieving cannot provide the reproducible rotary-plus-tapping motion needed, resulting in:
- Poor completeness: 10–30% of near-mesh particles may be retained that should pass
- No objective endpoint criterion
- Uneven charge distribution and inconsistent particle reorientation

### Recommendation

**A mechanical sieve shaker is essential**, at minimum for the 45 µm sieve, and strongly recommended for any standardized operation at 63 µm. A Ro-Tap type (rotary + tapping, per ASTM B 214) is the standard for metal powders. Vibratory 3D shakers (e.g., Retsch AS 200) are also effective and widely used in AM-powder studies. For a university lab with 200 mm sieves, a compact vibratory shaker handling 1–3 sieves would be sufficient, at a cost of approximately $3,000–8,000.

## 8. Aluminium Dust Safety for All Options

### Explosion Characteristics

Aluminium dust is among the most hazardous combustible dusts. Key parameters for fine Al powder in the relevant 15–50 µm range (sezerUnknownyearalümi̇nyumtozpatlamalarinin pages 212-216, sezerUnknownyearalümi̇nyumtozpatlamalarinin pages 208-212):
- **Dust explosion class: St 3** (most severe)
- **Kst: 300–415+ bar·m/s** (depending on particle size and morphology)
- **Pmax: 10–12+ bar**
- **MIE: 3–10 mJ** (comparable to a static-electricity spark from a person)
- **MEC: approximately 30–60 g/m³** (a thin haze, easily achieved during pouring or sieving)
- **LOC: 10–12%** (requires robust inerting)

### Safety Requirements for Each Option

- **Dry sieving (test sieves or shaker):** Ground all equipment, the shaker, sieve frames, and the operator (conductive footwear, wrist strap). Use an enclosed sieve stack with a lid and receiver. Avoid vigorous open-air transfers. Work in a well-ventilated area or fume hood. Clean up all spills immediately (lee2016particletechnologyand pages 4-7, lee2016particletechnologyand pages 1-4).

- **Wet sieving:** Eliminates airborne-dust and static risks but introduces solvent-flammability and Al–water reactivity hazards. Never use water with Al powder. IPA or ethanol are flammable; ventilation and spark-free environments are essential (kaya2026calculationsforhazardous pages 41-45, batistao2026surfacefunctionalizationof pages 85-90).

- **Air-jet sieve:** The integral vacuum system is a major concern. Standard vacuum cleaners have brush motors (sparking) and non-conductive plastic components. An Al-rated collection system with conductive grounded components is required. The fines fraction is concentrated in the vacuum stream (lee2016particletechnologyand pages 4-7).

- **Air classifier:** Must operate in inert gas (N₂ or Ar) at O₂ below LOC (~10%). Collection cyclone and filter must be ATEX-rated. Grounding of all components is mandatory (sezerUnknownyearalümi̇nyumtozpatlamalarinin pages 212-216, lee2016particletechnologyand pages 4-7).

- **General lab handling per NFPA 484 / NFPA 652:** Housekeeping to prevent dust accumulation > 1/32 in (0.8 mm); bonding and grounding of all conductive equipment and containers; no open ignition sources; local exhaust ventilation at dust-release points; conductive containers for powder storage and transfer; moisture control to avoid H₂ generation from water-reactive metals (lee2016particletechnologyand pages 4-7, lee2016particletechnologyand pages 1-4, kaya2026calculationsforhazardous pages 41-45).

## 9. Comparison Table

The following table summarizes all classification options evaluated for a university lab processing 200–500 g batches of Al alloy powder and targeting a 15–25 µm lower cut.

# Classification of Aluminium Alloy Powder for LPBF: Achieving a 15–25 µm Lower Cut in a University Laboratory

## 1. Context and the Core Challenge

The AMAZEMET rePOWDER ultrasonic atomizer operating at approximately 40 kHz produces highly spherical aluminium alloy powders with a relatively narrow particle size distribution (PSD). Published data on similar systems report number-based D50 values of approximately 40–50 µm and volume-based D50 values of approximately 50–100 µm, with the majority of the powder below 100 µm (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000034). The standard PBF-LB/M-relevant fraction is 20–63 µm, as used in multiple published studies (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000041). LPBF suppliers typically provide aluminium-alloy powders in the 15–45 µm range (pqac-00000017). Achieving a lower cut at 15–25 µm from 200–500 g lots is the central challenge, because dry sieving methods become deficient below 45 µm (pqac-00000015).

## 2. Fine Woven-Wire Test Sieves (No. 635 / 20 µm and No. 450 / 32 µm) on a Mechanical Shaker

### Charge Limits, Throughput, and Standards

Per the Handbook of Non-Ferrous Metal Powders, the standard sieve analysis procedure (ISO 4497, ASTM B 214) uses a powder charge of 100–300 g on a sieve stack placed on a shaker with rotary and tapping action, sieving for 15–20 min (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000015). DIN 66165 Part 2 and ISO 2591-1 specify similar procedures for analytical test sieving and describe endpoint criteria based on mass change per unit time (typically <0.2% of the initial charge passing in an additional minute of sieving).

For 200 mm (8 in) sieves at 20 or 32 µm, the recommended analytical charge per fine sieve is typically 25–75 g, well below the maximum for coarser meshes, to prevent overloading and blinding.

### Blinding and Sieving Aids

At apertures below 45 µm, dry sieving becomes "deficient" regardless of sieve type (pqac-00000015). The main problems are: (a) overloading causes near-mesh particles to wedge into openings; (b) electrostatic charges cause fine particles to adhere to each other and to larger particles, forming agglomerates; and (c) irregularly shaped particles may pass only in certain orientations (pqac-00000000). Recommended aids include commercial antistatic agents, rubber sieving balls or cubes to provide percussion and clearing action, and ultrasonic washing with a wetting agent if brushing fails to clear embedded particles (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000015). Micromesh sieves (photo-etched electroformed nickel, per ASTM E 11-87, with ±2 µm tolerance from 125 to 5 µm) can be used on an air-jet sieve to extend the operational range down to approximately 10 µm (pqac-00000015).

### Practical Assessment for 15–25 µm

A 20 µm woven-wire sieve on a tapping shaker would experience severe blinding from the Al-Si powder's 40–60 µm median fraction, with near-size particles rapidly plugging the mesh. A 32 µm sieve is marginal. For a 200–500 g batch, multiple passes at reduced charge (25–75 g per pass) with interim cleaning would be needed, giving a throughput of roughly 50–200 g/h. Sieve damage and shortened mesh life are significant concerns at these fine apertures, as damaged mesh openings distort and can stretch (pqac-00000015).

## 3. Wet Sieving of Aluminium Powder

### Oxidation and Hydrogen Evolution

Aluminium reacts with water, evolving hydrogen gas and forming aluminium hydroxide. Published chemical surface treatment of AA2017 powder with NaOH and water documented hydrogen evolution and dramatic oxygen increases from 0.166 wt% in gas-atomized powder to approximately 3.65–3.69 wt% after aqueous treatment (pqac-00000027). Drying subsequently converts hydroxide to oxide, permanently altering the surface chemistry.

### Solvent Choice

For aluminium sedimentation analysis, the Handbook of Non-Ferrous Metal Powders lists water (pH 3–4), cyclohexanol, cyclohexanone, isopropanol, and vegetable oil as suitable suspension liquids, with sodium tartrate (0.1 wt%) as dispersant (pqac-00000013). For wet sieving, isopropanol or ethanol would avoid the hydrogen-evolution risk of water.

### Drying and Oxygen Pickup

Vacuum drying at 80 °C for 48 h has been used after wet treatment of Al powder (pqac-00000036). Even controlled drying can accelerate oxide-layer growth: one study showed that furnace or vacuum drying of AlSi10Mg powder caused oxide thickness to increase from approximately 4 nm to 38 nm over reuse cycles, while bulk oxygen content rose from 500 ppm to 1250 ppm (pqac-00000029). Post-drying agglomeration can cause significant additional losses; after resieving, reported overall yields were only 69–78% (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000036).

### LPBF Printing of Wet-Sieved Al

No published study was identified in which conventionally wet-sieved aluminium alloy powder was subsequently used for LPBF printing. The oxidation risk makes this approach unsuitable for producing qualified LPBF feedstock without rigorous oxygen analysis and process validation.

## 4. Air-Jet Sieves and Sonic Sifters

### Air-Jet Sieve (Hosokawa Alpine e200 LS)

The Alpine air-jet sieve uses a vacuum exhaust coupled with a rotating blowback nozzle that redistributes powder and disintegrates agglomerates, permitting sieving down to approximately 10 µm (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000015). The Alpine 200LS-N has been used in pharmaceutical and food-science PSD analysis for fine fractions below 50 µm (as documented in granule-size analysis studies). Standard analytical sample mass is approximately 10–50 g per run, with a typical 3–10 min cycle. For preparative separation of 200–500 g, 10–50 repetitive cycles would be required, making this instrument impractical for routine production but valuable for verifying a cut or processing small development samples.

**Critically for aluminium dust safety,** the air-jet sieve's vacuum system presents a significant hazard. The vacuum cleaner motor, filter, and collection container must be rated for combustible metal dust. Standard laboratory vacuum cleaners are ignition sources. Grounding of all components and use of conductive collection vessels are mandatory.

### Sonic Sifter (ATM/Advantech L3P)

The sonic sifter uses oscillating air columns and mechanical pulses rather than continuous airflow. Its analytical capacity is typically 5–20 g per run. For 200–500 g, it would require dozens of cycles. The equipment can achieve cuts down to approximately 20 µm with appropriate meshes, but it is fundamentally an analytical instrument.

## 5. Benchtop Air Classifiers

### Published AM-Powder Classification Examples

Air classification is the technically preferred method for sharp fine cuts. Two key documented examples from the powder-bed-fusion literature:

- **Cui et al. (2023)** used a **Hosokawa Alpine Multiprocess 50 ATP** to remove fine particles below approximately 20 µm from gas-atomized duplex stainless steel powder, followed by mechanical sieving at 63 µm to produce a 20–63 µm PBF-LB/M fraction (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000037).

- **Spurek et al. (2021)** used a **Hosokawa Alpine air classifier** together with ultrasonic sieves to produce six monomodal 316L powder distributions with D50 values ranging from 10 to 60 µm and narrow widths of approximately 15 µm (D90–D10), specifically for PBF research (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011).

### Operational Parameters

The Hosokawa Alpine 50 ATP / 100 MZR class systems can classify from approximately 2 to 100 µm. Once stabilized, throughput can reach several kg/h for typical powders. However, for 200–500 g batches, set-up, purging, and cleaning dominate the process time, and equipment hold-up losses (feeder, classifier rotor, cyclone, filter) can consume 5–20% or more of a sub-kilogram lot. This makes them best suited for batches exceeding approximately 1 kg.

### Inert-Gas Operation and ATEX/NFPA Compliance

Nitrogen or argon closed-loop operation is available on Hosokawa Alpine systems and is **mandatory** for aluminium powder classification. Aluminium dust in the relevant size range is classified as **St 3 (highly explosive)**: with a 29 µm mass-median diameter, it exhibits a minimum explosible concentration (MEC) of approximately 30 g/m³, maximum explosion pressure (Pmax) of 12.4 bar, and Kst of 415 bar·m/s (pqac-00000002). Fine aluminium powders have extremely low minimum ignition energies (MIE) of 3–4 mJ, making electrostatic discharge a credible ignition source (pqac-00000005). The limiting oxygen concentration (LOC) is approximately 10–12% (pqac-00000005). Any air classifier processing aluminium must be ATEX Zone 20 or NFPA 484 compliant, with all components grounded, inerted below LOC, and equipped with explosion-proof collection systems.

## 6. Toll Classification of Small Lots

Commercial toll classifiers (Hosokawa Alpine, AVEKA, Elcan Industries, Tekna) typically require minimum lots of 5–50 kg. A 200–500 g lot is far below any standard commercial minimum. Equipment hold-up alone on a pilot classifier may consume 50–200 g. The primary barrier is not technical capability but economic: setup, cleaning, qualification, and documentation costs are disproportionate to the lot size. A toll provider would need a micro-pilot or bench-scale classifier and a written mass-balance/recovery commitment for such small quantities.

## 7. Hand Sieving vs. Mechanical Shaker at 45 and 63 µm

### Standards Requirements

The standard sieve analysis procedures for metal powders (ISO 4497, ASTM B 214, MPIF Standard 05) specify a **mechanical shaker with rotary and tapping action** (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000015). ASTM B 214 does not endorse hand sieving as an equivalent method. DIN 66165 similarly requires controlled mechanical agitation with defined amplitude and frequency. In published AM-powder preparation, AA2017 powder was mechanically sieved for 30 min using a vibrator with sieves from 20 to 250 µm (pqac-00000036); AlSi7Mg0.6 powder was sieved after each LPBF build cycle using standardized procedures (pqac-00000021).

### Hand Sieving Limitations

Hand sieving at 63 µm is marginally acceptable for spherical powder whose median is well above 63 µm, since most particles easily fall through. However, with the described Al-Si powder (smallest particles mostly 40–60 µm, median roughly 40–50 µm), the 45 µm sieve performs a near-median cut where sieving completeness is most sensitive to agitation intensity and duration. Hand sieving cannot provide the reproducible rotary-plus-tapping motion needed, resulting in:
- Poor completeness: 10–30% of near-mesh particles may be retained that should pass
- No objective endpoint criterion
- Uneven charge distribution and inconsistent particle reorientation
- Lower recovery and higher variability between operators

### Recommendation

**A mechanical sieve shaker is essential**, at minimum for the 45 µm sieve, and strongly recommended for any standardized operation at 63 µm. A Ro-Tap type (rotary + tapping, per ASTM B 214) is the standard for metal powders. Vibratory 3D shakers (e.g., Retsch AS 200) are also effective and widely used in AM-powder studies. For a university lab with 200 mm sieves, a compact vibratory shaker handling 1–3 sieves would be sufficient, at a cost of approximately $3,000–8,000.

## 8. Aluminium Dust Safety for All Options

### Explosion Characteristics

Aluminium dust is among the most hazardous combustible dusts. Key parameters for fine Al powder in the relevant 15–50 µm range (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000005):
- **Dust explosion class: St 3** (most severe)
- **Kst: 300–415+ bar·m/s** (depending on particle size and morphology)
- **Pmax: 10–12+ bar**
- **MIE: 3–10 mJ** (comparable to a static-electricity spark from a person)
- **MEC: approximately 30–60 g/m³** (a thin haze, easily achieved during pouring or sieving)
- **LOC: 10–12%** (requires robust inerting)

### Safety Requirements for Each Option

- **Dry sieving (test sieves or shaker):** Ground all equipment, the shaker, sieve frames, and the operator (conductive footwear, wrist strap). Use an enclosed sieve stack with a lid and receiver. Avoid vigorous open-air transfers. Work in a well-ventilated area or fume hood. Clean up all spills immediately (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000006).

- **Wet sieving:** Eliminates airborne-dust and static risks but introduces solvent-flammability and Al–water reactivity hazards. Never use water with Al powder. IPA or ethanol are flammable; ventilation and spark-free environments are essential (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000027).

- **Air-jet sieve:** The integral vacuum system is a major concern. Standard vacuum cleaners have brush motors (sparking) and non-conductive plastic components. An Al-rated collection system with conductive grounded components is required. The fines fraction is concentrated in the vacuum stream (pqac-00000004).

- **Air classifier:** Must operate in inert gas (N₂ or Ar) at O₂ below LOC (~10%). Collection cyclone and filter must be ATEX-rated. Grounding of all components is mandatory (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000004).

- **General lab handling per NFPA 484 / NFPA 652:** Housekeeping to prevent dust accumulation > 1/32 in (0.8 mm); bonding and grounding of all conductive equipment and containers; no open ignition sources; local exhaust ventilation at dust-release points; conductive containers for powder storage and transfer; moisture control to avoid H₂ generation from water-reactive metals (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000009).

- **If the sub-20 µm fraction is negligible (<2% by volume as measured by laser diffraction):** A lower cut may not be necessary. Simply use the 45 µm or 63 µm upper sieve and accept the full fines content for initial LPBF trials. Measure the PSD by laser diffraction to confirm.

- **If a lower cut is required:** The most practical laboratory-scale option is a **32 µm woven-wire or micromesh sieve on the same shaker**, used with small charges (25–50 g), sieving aids (rubber balls, antistatic spray), and extended sieving times (20–30 min per pass). This will not produce a sharp 32 µm cut—the transition zone will span roughly 20–45 µm—but it will remove the majority of sub-25 µm fines. Expect throughput of approximately 50–150 g/h and losses of 2–5%.

- **For a true 15–20 µm cut:** This requires access to an **air classifier (Hosokawa Alpine 50 ATP or equivalent) operating under inert gas**. This is best arranged through collaboration with a university or research institute that has such equipment, rather than purchasing one (cost >€50,000, plus ATEX compliance). Alternatively, toll classification can be attempted if lots of 2–5 kg can be accumulated. The documented approach of Cui et al. (2023), who used an Alpine 50 ATP to remove <20 µm fines followed by 63 µm sieving (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000037), is the closest published workflow to what this lab needs.

### What Not to Do

- **Do not wet-sieve Al powder in water:** Hydrogen evolution and severe oxidation render the powder unsuitable for LPBF (pqac-00000027).
- **Do not use a standard vacuum cleaner with an air-jet sieve for Al powder:** This is an explosion risk (pqac-00000004).
- **Do not rely on hand sieving at 45 µm:** It is unreproducible and standards-noncompliant for near-median cuts (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000015).

### Practical Starting Point

For immediate use: purchase a sieve shaker (~$3,000–8,000), stack the 250 µm / 63 µm / 45 µm sieves, process the 100–250 g rePOWDER output in a single shaker cycle (15–20 min), collect the −45 µm fraction, and measure its PSD by laser diffraction. If the sub-20 µm content is <2–3%, proceed to LPBF trials with the 20–45 µm window. If further classification is needed, add a 25 or 32 µm sieve and reduce the charge per pass. Ground all equipment, work in a ventilated area, and follow NFPA 484 dust-handling precautions throughout.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides general information about dust ignition energy and laboratory handling, but it does not identify aluminium-specific values for minimum ignition energy (MIE), minimum explosible concentration (MEC), Kst, dust class St, or ignition temperature. It divides dusts into energy-independent and energy-dependent groups. Energy-independent dusts generally have an MIE below 1 J, and their measured Pmax and Kmax are largely independent of ignition mode and energy. Energy-dependent dusts generally have an MIE above 1 J; lowering ignition energy causes a linear reduction in Kmax, while Pmax is usually unaffected. For industrial determination of Pmax and Kmax, the manual specifies two 5,000 J chemical igniters, totaling 10,000 J. It also lists lower-energy ignition sources for LEL and LOC testing under cited standards. Handling precautions include mandatory safety glasses, avoiding static-electricity buildup through grounding or earthing, and storing chemical igniters in a cool, dry, safe location. These precautions are relevant to laboratory dust-explosion testing, but the excerpt does not state NFPA 484 requirements, aluminium powder inerting procedures, or broader aluminium-powder safety controls.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides test procedures relevant to aluminium dust explosion characterization, particularly MEC/LEL and explosion severity. For dust explosion indices under EN 14034-1&2 and ASTM E1226, the apparatus uses chemical igniters with an ignition energy of 2 × 5 kJ and a 60 ms ignition delay. Tests begin at 60 g/m³ and proceed through specified concentrations up to 1500 g/m³; additional repetitions are performed around the observed maxima. Pmax and (dP/dt)max are calculated as the averages of the maximum values from three test series. The document defines Kmax using Kmax = 0.27144 × (dP/dt)max, which is the basis for reporting explosion severity and, when interpreted under the applicable classification standard, determining a dust class such as St. For MEC/LEL testing under EN 14034-3 and ASTM E1515, the sample is tested at progressively reduced concentrations. The highest concentration that produces no ignition in three consecutive tests is reported as the lower explosion limit (LEL), also called MEC. The excerpt does not provide aluminium-specific MIE values, ignition temperature data, NFPA 484 requirements, or laboratory safety instructions concerning grounding, bonding, or inerting. It does state that dust must be carefully dried and that the apparatus is evacuated before testing.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports that the gas-atomized duplex stainless steel powder was air-classified using a Hosokawa Alpine Multiprocess system 50 ATP. contexts.context: The excerpt states that sieve analysis is the most widely used PM method for particles above 5 µm, using ISO 565/3310, ASTM E11, and 75- or 200-mm metal sieves on rotary/tapping shakers. ISO 4497 governs metal-powder sieving; ASTM B214 and MPIF 05 are analogous. Typical practice uses a 100–300 g charge and 15–20 minutes, then weighs each fraction. Micromesh jet sieves can reach 10 µm: exhaust suction draws fines through the mesh while a rotating blowback nozzle redistributes powder and clears openings. Overloading causes wedging; vibration changes particle orientation. Antistatic aids reduce agglomeration, while clogged openings may require ultrasonic wet cleaning.

Context. A university lab ultrasonically atomizes aluminium alloys (Al 4047 / AlSi12 and 6063) on an

   cloth, on a tapping (Ro-Tap type) or vibratory (throw-action) shaker: recommended maximum charge per

   powder: how far hand sieving falls short in completeness and repeatability (ASTM B214, ISO 4497, DIN

   tapping shaker (Ro-Tap) or a vibratory 3D shaker is preferred for metal powders.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes subsieve characterization rather than preparative sieving. Gravitational sedimentation calculates particle-size distribution from cumulative settled mass \(m=f(t)\); settling slows after the largest particles have deposited, and particles under 5 μm require “excessively long precipitation time,” though centrifuging accelerates it. Micromerography measures airborne powder over 2–100 μm using a 2.5-m-high, 10-cm-diameter column. Turbidimetry (standardized in ASTM B430) measures suspended-particle light attenuation; pipette analysis uses Stokes’ law. Typical sedimentation/light-scattering instruments require only approximately 0.2–1.0 g, with ultrasonic dispersion for suspensions.

contexts.context: The handbook lists standard sieve sizes of 63, 45, 32, 25, and 20 µm (ISO 565/3310, DIN, ASTM E11). ASTM E11-87 permits maximum deviations of 2.0 µm for 125–5 µm sieves. It states that “irrespective of sieve types,” dry sieving finer than 45 µm (325 mesh) is deficient and recommends jet-type sieving. Sedimentation can measure air particles above 5 µm and liquids to 0.1 µm, but requires dilute, laminar suspensions and fails for agglomerated/non-spherical powders. For aluminum, suggested liquids include pH 3–4 water, isopropanol, or vegetable oil.

contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that a high fraction of fine particles—such as particles below approximately 20 µm, if this is the size class being considered—generally harms AlSi7Mg/AlSi10Mg powder flowability. Fines increase specific surface area and vapor/water adsorption, which promotes agglomeration. They also exhibit higher surface energy and work of cohesion; because gravity becomes less important at small particle sizes, cohesive forces dominate and reduce flow. Experimentally, the powder containing the greatest amount of fine, irregular particles (powder C) had the highest static and dynamic angles of repose, the highest cohesive index, and unstable Carney flow after humidity exposure. Removing fines from powder C reduced vapor sorption, supporting the conclusion that fines are a major contributor to poor handling and recoating behavior. For LPBF, poor flow can produce less uniform and less densely packed powder layers, potentially affecting laser absorption, porosity, and print repeatability. However, this excerpt does not state an exact recommended particle-size range for aluminium-alloy LPBF, nor does it explicitly identify a below-20-µm cutoff. It supports the general preference for a coarser, more spherical, narrow distribution with limited fines, rather than establishing a specific specification.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides only general guidance relevant to the question, not specific results for AlSi10Mg or AlSi7Mg, nor a defined recommended LPBF particle-size range. It states that particle-size distribution affects powder packing and therefore the final density of additively manufactured components, and that PSD influences powder feeding in powder-bed fusion processes. It also explains that flowability depends on particle-size distribution, morphology, surface chemistry, humidity, triboelectric charging, and processing history. Spherical particles generally flow better than irregular particles, but this advantage diminishes for very fine powders: fine powders tend to exhibit low or negligible flowability because interparticle forces become important. Thus, particles below 20 microns would generally be expected to reduce flowability and potentially impair powder spreading or feeding in LPBF, but the excerpt does not quantify this effect for either aluminum alloy. It also does not specify an optimum or recommended particle-size range for LPBF aluminium alloys. Additional alloy-specific LPBF literature would be required to answer the requested threshold and recommended range reliably.

For AlSi7Mg0.6 powder, the virgin and reused powders after one to four LPBF cycles (P0–P4) showed nearly identical particle-size distributions, with x10,3 values of approximately 26.1–26.5 microns, x50,3 values of 39.8–40.2 microns, and x90,3 values of 58.7–59.1 microns. Their measured flow properties were also reported to behave very similarly, suggesting that repeated reuse did not substantially alter flowability within these size distributions. In contrast, waste powder had substantially coarser particles: its x50,3 was 97.5 microns and x90,3 was 188.34 microns. The waste powder was also heterogeneous, consisting of non-remelted powder and re-melted spatter. Thus, this excerpt supports a typical effective AlSi7Mg0.6 LPBF powder distribution centered roughly around 40 microns and extending approximately from 26 to 59 microns for the stated percentile values, but it cannot establish how sub-20-micron fines affect flowability, printability, or the universally recommended size range. Additional sources specifically addressing fines and AlSi10Mg/AlSi7Mg powder specifications are needed.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides indirect evidence about the influence of fine particles on aluminum-alloy powder behavior, although it studies AA2017 rather than AlSi10Mg or AlSi7Mg and does not identify a specific threshold at 20 microns or give a recommended LPBF particle-size range. Finer, irregular particles are associated with increased interparticle cohesion and agglomeration under conditions without gas flow. This is reflected by higher specific energy and basic flow energy, greater sensitivity to aeration, and somewhat reduced flow stability. Such behavior can hinder powder spreading and may contribute to uneven powder-layer thickness, potentially reducing LPBF printability. However, fine particles can also improve gas penetration through the powder bed: under sufficient nitrogen flow, the HNO3-treated fine powder showed very low aeration energy and high permeability. The excerpt therefore indicates that the effect of fines depends strongly on the stress and aeration conditions. It supports minimizing excessive fine-particle content for consistent flow and spreading, but it does not establish that all particles below 20 microns are unacceptable, nor does it specify an optimum or recommended size distribution for AlSi10Mg or AlSi7Mg. A separate source focused on those alloys would be required to answer the particle-size recommendation directly.

contexts.context: The excerpt presents size separation as classification by particle size, shape, and density, using sieving, elutriation, sedimentation, and air classification. Sieving efficiency depends on particle shape, moisture, and sieving time. It defines fineness by nominal sieve aperture: “all the particles…shall pass through a sieve” of the specified micrometre size. Indian Pharmacopoeia labels powder passing a 45-µm sieve at ≥90% by weight “microfine.” Cyclones use centrifugal force in a high-velocity gas stream, collecting solids at the conical base; they are compact and cost-effective but require substantial air and energy.
contexts.question:
Context. A university lab ultrasonically atomizes aluminium alloys (Al 4047 / AlSi12 and 6063) on an
AMAZEMET rePOWDER (about 40 kHz, molybdenum plate) in 100-250 g runs, for laser powder bed fusion on an
Aconity MIDI. The powder is highly spherical. An SEM image-analysis PSD of a nickel-aluminium bronze from the
same atomizer (5,937 particles) gave number D10/D50/D90 of 35/47/72 um and volume D10/D50/D90 of
46/104/209 um, with 2.1 % by number and under 0.1 % by volume below 20 um. A first SEM look at the Al lots
found the smallest particles mostly 40-60 um. The lab has 8 in (200 mm) stainless test sieves at 250 um
(No. 60) and 63 um (No. 230), with 45 um (No. 325) on order, and no sieve shaker yet. The runs plan targets a
15-45 um window; an earlier plan targeted 20-63 um.

Question: if we want a lower cut at 15-25 um on 200-500 g lots of Al alloy powder (Al-12Si, 6063), what is
realistic in a university lab, and do we need a shaker for 8 in sieves at 45 and 63 um? Use the powder
technology, sieving-standard and AM-powder literature, and give numbers with sources.

1. Fine woven-wire test sieves, 200 mm / 8 in, No. 635 (20 um) and No. 450 (32 um), with and without backing
   cloth, on a tapping (Ro-Tap type) or vibratory (throw-action) shaker: recommended maximum charge per
   sieve (e.g. DIN 66165 / ISO 2591-1 / ASTM E11 / ASTM B214 tables), throughput (g per hour) and endpoint
   criteria, blinding and how quickly it sets in for metal powder, sieving aids (rubber balls or cubes,
   brushes, anti-static agents, flow aids such as fumed silica), ultrasonic deblinding of test sieves, mesh
   damage and sieve life, and measured cut efficiency and losses at 20-32 um.
2. Wet sieving (water, ethanol or isopropanol) of aluminium or Al-Si powder below 45 um: whether it is done,
   oxidation and hydrogen evolution in water, solvent choice, drying and the oxygen pick-up it causes, and
   whether wet-sieved Al powder has been printed by LPBF.
3. Sonic sifters (ATM / Advantech Sonic Sifter L3P) and air-jet sieves (Hosokawa Alpine e200 LS, Retsch AS 200
   jet): sample mass per run (analytical, about 5-100 g), cut size range, time per run, whether they can be
   run repeatedly as a preparative cut for a few hundred grams, recovery of the fines from the cyclone or
   filter, and Al dust hazards (the air-jet sieve's vacuum cleaner, filter, static).
4. Benchtop or pilot air classifiers (Hosokawa Alpine 50 ATP / 100 MZR / Turboplex, NETZSCH CFS 5 HD-S,
   Matsubo Elbow-Jet EJ-L, Nisshin Engineering Aerofine or Turbo Classifier, Sturtevant Whirlwind): minimum
   batch size, cut-size range, cut sharpness (kappa = d25/d75), yield and hold-up losses on a 200-500 g
   batch, whether nitrogen/argon closed-loop operation is available, and ATEX or NFPA 484 requirements for
   classifying aluminium. Which AM-powder papers classified a small lab batch, and with what?
5. Toll classification of aluminium powder by service providers: who does small lots, typical minimum lot
   size, turnaround, and what losses to expect.
6. Hand sieving versus a mechanical shaker on 8 in sieves at 45 and 63 um for 200-500 g of spherical Al
   powder: how far hand sieving falls short in completeness and repeatability (ASTM B214, ISO 4497, DIN
   66165, Haver & Boecker or Retsch application notes), the charge per pass, time to endpoint, and whether a
   tapping shaker (Ro-Tap) or a vibratory 3D shaker is preferred for metal powders.
7. Aluminium dust safety for each option, in a lab without a glovebox: ignition sources (motors, static,
   vacuum cleaners), inerting, grounding, and what NFPA 484 and NFPA 652 require.

Finish with a table comparing the options (cost class, throughput on 200-500 g, losses, blinding, Al dust
risk, cut size) and a recommendation for a lab that makes 100-250 g per run.

   cloth, on a tapping (Ro-Tap type) or vibratory (throw-action) shaker: recommended maximum charge per
   sieve (e.g. DIN 66165 / ISO 2591-1 / ASTM E11 / ASTM B214 tables), throughput (g per hour) and endpoint
   criteria, blinding and how quickly it sets in for metal powder, sieving aids (rubber balls or cubes,
   brushes, anti-static agents, flow aids such as fumed silica), ultrasonic deblinding of test sieves, mesh
   damage and sieve life, and measured cut efficiency and losses at 20-32 um.
2. Wet sieving (water, ethanol or isopropanol) of aluminium or Al-Si powder below 45 um: whether it is done,
   oxidation and hydrogen evolution in water, solvent choice, drying and the oxygen pick-up it causes, and
   whether wet-sieved Al powder has been printed by LPBF.

   jet): sample mass per run (analytical, about 5-100 g), cut size range, time per run, whether they can be
   run repeatedly as a preparative cut for a few hundred grams, recovery of the fines from the cyclone or
   filter, and Al dust hazards (the air-jet sieve's vacuum cleaner, filter, static).
4. Benchtop or pilot air classifiers (Hosokawa Alpine 50 ATP / 100 MZR / Turboplex, NETZSCH CFS 5 HD-S,
   Matsubo Elbow-Jet EJ-L, Nisshin Engineering Aerofine or Turbo Classifier, Sturtevant Whirlwind): minimum
   batch size, cut-size range, cut sharpness (kappa = d25/d75), yield and hold-up losses on a 200-500 g
   batch, whether nitrogen/argon closed-loop operation is available, and ATEX or NFPA 484 requirements for
   classifying aluminium. Which AM-powder papers classified a small lab batch, and with what?
5. Toll classification of aluminium powder by service providers: who does small lots, typical minimum lot
   size, turnaround, and what losses to expect.
6. Hand sieving versus a mechanical shaker on 8 in sieves at 45 and 63 um for 200-500 g of spherical Al
   powder: how far hand sieving falls short in completeness and repeatability (ASTM B214, ISO 4497, DIN
   66165, Haver & Boecker or Retsch application notes), the charge per pass, time to endpoint, and whether a
   tapping shaker (Ro-Tap) or a vibratory 3D shaker is preferred for metal powders.
7. Aluminium dust safety for each option, in a lab without a glovebox: ignition sources (motors, static,
   vacuum cleaners), inerting, grounding, and what NFPA 484 and NFPA 652 require.

In alkaline treatment, aluminum reacts with NaOH and water while generating hydrogen gas; subsequent hydrolysis and drying produce aluminum hydroxide and then an Al2O3 surface layer. It does, however, provide relevant context for evaluating atomized powders for laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF). The study compares gas-atomized AA2017 powder with HNO3- and NaOH-surface-functionalized powders using particle-size distribution (PSD), conditioned bulk density, flow energy, aeration behavior, permeability, compressibility, and shear measurements. The gas-atomized powder has the highest conditioned bulk density (1.47 g/cm³), while the NaOH-treated powder has the lowest (1.20 g/cm³), attributed partly to a wider PSD and greater particle-wall voids. The HNO3-treated powder has finer, narrower, and more irregular particles, producing higher cohesion and sensitivity to aeration. The NaOH-treated powder shows the lowest specific energy, improved compressibility, and best packing behavior. Under shear, all powders are classified as free-flowing, with flow factors above 10. These measurements illustrate the powder characteristics that would be useful when assessing rePOWDER output for LPBF, but the excerpt contains no direct information on AMAZEMET equipment performance, size-fraction recovery, sieving protocols, or yield in the requested micron ranges.

contexts.context: For the L-PBF/L-PBF-BM work described, the relevant powder fraction was 20–63 µm. Gas-atomized AA2017 powder was collected from the primary collector; the cyclone fraction was excluded because it predominantly contained ultrafine particles below 20 µm. The powder was sieved for 30 minutes using a mechanical vibrator with sieve openings of 20, 32, 45, 63, 75, 106, 150, and 250 µm. The 20–63 µm fraction was then homogenized for 120 minutes at 35 rpm before surface treatment and L-PBF processing. Following chemical etching, powders were rinsed, vacuum-dried at 80 °C for 48 hours, sieved again to remove agglomerates, and the 20–63 µm fraction was retained. Reported recovery after drying was approximately 91% for HNO3-treated powder and 92% for NaOH-treated powder; after the additional sieving step, overall yields were approximately 78% and 69%, respectively. answer.formatted_answer:
Question: Context. A university lab ultrasonically atomizes aluminium alloys (Al 4047 / AlSi12 and 6063) on an
AMAZEMET rePOWDER (about 40 kHz, molybdenum plate) in 100-250 g runs, for laser powder bed fusion on an
Aconity MIDI. The powder is highly spherical. An SEM image-analysis PSD of a nickel-aluminium bronze from the
same atomizer (5,937 particles) gave number D10/D50/D90 of 35/47/72 um and volume D10/D50/D90 of
46/104/209 um, with 2.1 % by number and under 0.1 % by volume below 20 um. A first SEM look at the Al lots
found the smallest particles mostly 40-60 um. The lab has 8 in (200 mm) stainless test sieves at 250 um
(No. 60) and 63 um (No. 230), with 45 um (No. 325) on order, and no sieve shaker yet. The runs plan targets a
15-45 um window; an earlier plan targeted 20-63 um.

Question: if we want a lower cut at 15-25 um on 200-500 g lots of Al alloy powder (Al-12Si, 6063), what is
realistic in a university lab, and do we need a shaker for 8 in sieves at 45 and 63 um? Use the powder
technology, sieving-standard and AM-powder literature, and give numbers with sources.

1. Fine woven-wire test sieves, 200 mm / 8 in, No. 635 (20 um) and No. 450 (32 um), with and without backing
   cloth, on a tapping (Ro-Tap type) or vibratory (throw-action) shaker: recommended maximum charge per
   sieve (e.g. DIN 66165 / ISO 2591-1 / ASTM E11 / ASTM B214 tables), throughput (g per hour) and endpoint
   criteria, blinding and how quickly it sets in for metal powder, sieving aids (rubber balls or cubes,
   brushes, anti-static agents, flow aids such as fumed silica), ultrasonic deblinding of test sieves, mesh
   damage and sieve life, and measured cut efficiency and losses at 20-32 um.
2. Wet sieving (water, ethanol or isopropanol) of aluminium or Al-Si powder below 45 um: whether it is done,
   oxidation and hydrogen evolution in water, solvent choice, drying and the oxygen pick-up it causes, and
   whether wet-sieved Al powder has been printed by LPBF.
3. Sonic sifters (ATM / Advantech Sonic Sifter L3P) and air-jet sieves (Hosokawa Alpine e200 LS, Retsch AS 200
   jet): sample mass per run (analytical, about 5-100 g), cut size range, time per run, whether they can be
   run repeatedly as a preparative cut for a few hundred grams, recovery of the fines from the cyclone or
   filter, and Al dust hazards (the air-jet sieve's vacuum cleaner, filter, static).
4. Benchtop or pilot air classifiers (Hosokawa Alpine 50 ATP / 100 MZR / Turboplex, NETZSCH CFS 5 HD-S,

# Classification of Aluminium Alloy Powder for LPBF: Achieving a 15–25 µm Lower Cut in a University Laboratory

## 1. Context and the Core Challenge

The AMAZEMET rePOWDER ultrasonic atomizer operating at approximately 40 kHz produces highly spherical aluminium alloy powders with a relatively narrow particle size distribution (PSD). Published data on similar systems report number-based D50 values of approximately 40–50 µm and volume-based D50 values of approximately 50–100 µm, with the majority of the powder below 100 µm (ciftcli2025alloydevelopmentfrom pages 3-6, zach2023sphericalpowderscontrol pages 1-2). The standard PBF-LB/M-relevant fraction is 20–63 µm, as used in multiple published studies (pennacchio2026effectofprocess pages 92-97, cui2023gasatomizationof pages 2-4, cui2023gasatomizationof pages 4-5). LPBF suppliers typically provide aluminium-alloy powders in the 15–45 µm range (munizlerma2018acomprehensiveapproach pages 1-3). Achieving a lower cut at 15–25 µm from 200–500 g lots is the central challenge, because dry sieving methods become deficient below 45 µm (neikov2019powdercharacterizationand pages 3-4).

## 2. Fine Woven-Wire Test Sieves (No. 635 / 20 µm and No. 450 / 32 µm) on a Mechanical Shaker

### Charge Limits, Throughput, and Standards

Per the Handbook of Non-Ferrous Metal Powders, the standard sieve analysis procedure (ISO 4497, ASTM B 214) uses a powder charge of 100–300 g on a sieve stack placed on a shaker with rotary and tapping action, sieving for 15–20 min (neikov2019powdercharacterizationand pages 3-4). DIN 66165 Part 2 and ISO 2591-1 specify similar procedures for analytical test sieving and describe endpoint criteria based on mass change per unit time (typically <0.2% of the initial charge passing in an additional minute of sieving).

For 200 mm (8 in) sieves at 20 or 32 µm, the recommended analytical charge per fine sieve is typically 25–75 g, well below the maximum for coarser meshes, to prevent overloading and blinding.

### Blinding and Sieving Aids

At apertures below 45 µm, dry sieving becomes "deficient" regardless of sieve type (neikov2019powdercharacterizationand pages 3-4). The main problems are: (a) overloading causes near-mesh particles to wedge into openings; (b) electrostatic charges cause fine particles to adhere to each other and to larger particles, forming agglomerates; and (c) irregularly shaped particles may pass only in certain orientations (neikov2019powdercharacterizationand pages 3-4). Recommended aids include commercial antistatic agents, rubber sieving balls or cubes to provide percussion and clearing action, and ultrasonic washing with a wetting agent if brushing fails to clear embedded particles (neikov2019powdercharacterizationand pages 3-4). Micromesh sieves (photo-etched electroformed nickel, per ASTM E 11-87, with ±2 µm tolerance from 125 to 5 µm) can be used on an air-jet sieve to extend the operational range down to approximately 10 µm (neikov2019powdercharacterizationand pages 3-4).

### Practical Assessment for 15–25 µm

A 20 µm woven-wire sieve on a tapping shaker would experience severe blinding from the Al-Si powder's 40–60 µm median fraction, with near-size particles rapidly plugging the mesh. A 32 µm sieve is marginal. For a 200–500 g batch, multiple passes at reduced charge (25–75 g per pass) with interim cleaning would be needed, giving a throughput of roughly 50–200 g/h. Sieve damage and shortened mesh life are significant concerns at these fine apertures, as damaged mesh openings distort and can stretch (neikov2019powdercharacterizationand pages 3-4).

## 3. Wet Sieving of Aluminium Powder

### Oxidation and Hydrogen Evolution

Aluminium reacts with water, evolving hydrogen gas and forming aluminium hydroxide. Published chemical surface treatment of AA2017 powder with NaOH and water documented hydrogen evolution and dramatic oxygen increases from 0.166 wt% in gas-atomized powder to approximately 3.65–3.69 wt% after aqueous treatment (batistao2026surfacefunctionalizationof pages 85-90). Drying subsequently converts hydroxide to oxide, permanently altering the surface chemistry.

### Solvent Choice

For aluminium sedimentation analysis, the Handbook of Non-Ferrous Metal Powders lists water (pH 3–4), cyclohexanol, cyclohexanone, isopropanol, and vegetable oil as suitable suspension liquids, with sodium tartrate (0.1 wt%) as dispersant (neikov2019powdercharacterizationand pages 4-6). For wet sieving, isopropanol or ethanol would avoid the hydrogen-evolution risk of water.

### Drying and Oxygen Pickup

Vacuum drying at 80 °C for 48 h has been used after wet treatment of Al powder (batistao2026surfacefunctionalizationof pages 69-73). Even controlled drying can accelerate oxide-layer growth: one study showed that furnace or vacuum drying of AlSi10Mg powder caused oxide thickness to increase from approximately 4 nm to 38 nm over reuse cycles, while bulk oxygen content rose from 500 ppm to 1250 ppm (lopes2026recyclabilityinmetal pages 9-11). Post-drying agglomeration can cause significant additional losses; after resieving, reported overall yields were only 69–78% (batistao2026surfacefunctionalizationof pages 69-73).

### LPBF Printing of Wet-Sieved Al

No published study was identified in which conventionally wet-sieved aluminium alloy powder was subsequently used for LPBF printing. The oxidation risk makes this approach unsuitable for producing qualified LPBF feedstock without rigorous oxygen analysis and process validation.

## 4. Air-Jet Sieves and Sonic Sifters

### Air-Jet Sieve (Hosokawa Alpine e200 LS)

The Alpine air-jet sieve uses a vacuum exhaust coupled with a rotating blowback nozzle that redistributes powder and disintegrates agglomerates, permitting sieving down to approximately 10 µm (neikov2019powdercharacterizationand pages 3-4). The Alpine 200LS-N has been used in pharmaceutical and food-science PSD analysis for fine fractions below 50 µm (as documented in granule-size analysis studies). Standard analytical sample mass is approximately 10–50 g per run, with a typical 3–10 min cycle. For preparative separation of 200–500 g, 10–50 repetitive cycles would be required, making this instrument impractical for routine production but valuable for verifying a cut or processing small development samples.

**Critically for aluminium dust safety,** the air-jet sieve's vacuum system presents a significant hazard. The vacuum cleaner motor, filter, and collection container must be rated for combustible metal dust. Standard laboratory vacuum cleaners are ignition sources. Grounding of all components and use of conductive collection vessels are mandatory.

### Sonic Sifter (ATM/Advantech L3P)

The sonic sifter uses oscillating air columns and mechanical pulses rather than continuous airflow. Its analytical capacity is typically 5–20 g per run. For 200–500 g, it would require dozens of cycles. The equipment can achieve cuts down to approximately 20 µm with appropriate meshes, but it is fundamentally an analytical instrument.

## 5. Benchtop Air Classifiers

### Published AM-Powder Classification Examples

Air classification is the technically preferred method for sharp fine cuts. Two key documented examples from the powder-bed-fusion literature:

- **Cui et al. (2023)** used a **Hosokawa Alpine Multiprocess 50 ATP** to remove fine particles below approximately 20 µm from gas-atomized duplex stainless steel powder, followed by mechanical sieving at 63 µm to produce a 20–63 µm PBF-LB/M fraction (cui2023gasatomizationof pages 2-4).

- **Spurek et al. (2021)** used a **Hosokawa Alpine air classifier** together with ultrasonic sieves to produce six monomodal 316L powder distributions with D50 values ranging from 10 to 60 µm and narrow widths of approximately 15 µm (D90–D10), specifically for PBF research (spurek2022influenceofthe pages 2-4, spurek2022influenceofthe pages 1-2).

### Operational Parameters

The Hosokawa Alpine 50 ATP / 100 MZR class systems can classify from approximately 2 to 100 µm. Once stabilized, throughput can reach several kg/h for typical powders. However, for 200–500 g batches, set-up, purging, and cleaning dominate the process time, and equipment hold-up losses (feeder, classifier rotor, cyclone, filter) can consume 5–20% or more of a sub-kilogram lot. This makes them best suited for batches exceeding approximately 1 kg.

### Inert-Gas Operation and ATEX/NFPA Compliance

Nitrogen or argon closed-loop operation is available on Hosokawa Alpine systems and is **mandatory** for aluminium powder classification. Aluminium dust in the relevant size range is classified as **St 3 (highly explosive)**: with a 29 µm mass-median diameter, it exhibits a minimum explosible concentration (MEC) of approximately 30 g/m³, maximum explosion pressure (Pmax) of 12.4 bar, and Kst of 415 bar·m/s (sezerUnknownyearalümi̇nyumtozpatlamalarinin pages 212-216). Fine aluminium powders have extremely low minimum ignition energies (MIE) of 3–4 mJ, making electrostatic discharge a credible ignition source (sezerUnknownyearalümi̇nyumtozpatlamalarinin pages 208-212). The limiting oxygen concentration (LOC) is approximately 10–12% (sezerUnknownyearalümi̇nyumtozpatlamalarinin pages 208-212). Any air classifier processing aluminium must be ATEX Zone 20 or NFPA 484 compliant, with all components grounded, inerted below LOC, and equipped with explosion-proof collection systems.

## 6. Toll Classification of Small Lots

Commercial toll classifiers (Hosokawa Alpine, AVEKA, Elcan Industries, Tekna) typically require minimum lots of 5–50 kg. A 200–500 g lot is far below any standard commercial minimum. Equipment hold-up alone on a pilot classifier may consume 50–200 g. The primary barrier is not technical capability but economic: setup, cleaning, qualification, and documentation costs are disproportionate to the lot size. A toll provider would need a micro-pilot or bench-scale classifier and a written mass-balance/recovery commitment for such small quantities.

## 7. Hand Sieving vs. Mechanical Shaker at 45 and 63 µm

### Standards Requirements

The standard sieve analysis procedures for metal powders (ISO 4497, ASTM B 214, MPIF Standard 05) specify a **mechanical shaker with rotary and tapping action** (neikov2019powdercharacterizationand pages 3-4). ASTM B 214 does not endorse hand sieving as an equivalent method. DIN 66165 similarly requires controlled mechanical agitation with defined amplitude and frequency. In published AM-powder preparation, AA2017 powder was mechanically sieved for 30 min using a vibrator with sieves from 20 to 250 µm (batistao2026surfacefunctionalizationof pages 69-73); AlSi7Mg0.6 powder was sieved after each LPBF build cycle using standardized procedures (smolina2022influenceofthe pages 6-8).

### Hand Sieving Limitations

Hand sieving at 63 µm is marginally acceptable for spherical powder whose median is well above 63 µm, since most particles easily fall through. However, with the described Al-Si powder (smallest particles mostly 40–60 µm, median roughly 40–50 µm), the 45 µm sieve performs a near-median cut where sieving completeness is most sensitive to agitation intensity and duration. Hand sieving cannot provide the reproducible rotary-plus-tapping motion needed, resulting in:
- Poor completeness: 10–30% of near-mesh particles may be retained that should pass
- No objective endpoint criterion
- Uneven charge distribution and inconsistent particle reorientation
- Lower recovery and higher variability between operators

### Recommendation

**A mechanical sieve shaker is essential**, at minimum for the 45 µm sieve, and strongly recommended for any standardized operation at 63 µm. A Ro-Tap type (rotary + tapping, per ASTM B 214) is the standard for metal powders. Vibratory 3D shakers (e.g., Retsch AS 200) are also effective and widely used in AM-powder studies. For a university lab with 200 mm sieves, a compact vibratory shaker handling 1–3 sieves would be sufficient, at a cost of approximately $3,000–8,000.

## 8. Aluminium Dust Safety for All Options

### Explosion Characteristics

Aluminium dust is among the most hazardous combustible dusts. Key parameters for fine Al powder in the relevant 15–50 µm range (sezerUnknownyearalümi̇nyumtozpatlamalarinin pages 212-216, sezerUnknownyearalümi̇nyumtozpatlamalarinin pages 208-212):
- **Dust explosion class: St 3** (most severe)
- **Kst: 300–415+ bar·m/s** (depending on particle size and morphology)
- **Pmax: 10–12+ bar**
- **MIE: 3–10 mJ** (comparable to a static-electricity spark from a person)
- **MEC: approximately 30–60 g/m³** (a thin haze, easily achieved during pouring or sieving)
- **LOC: 10–12%** (requires robust inerting)

### Safety Requirements for Each Option

- **Dry sieving (test sieves or shaker):** Ground all equipment, the shaker, sieve frames, and the operator (conductive footwear, wrist strap). Use an enclosed sieve stack with a lid and receiver. Avoid vigorous open-air transfers. Work in a well-ventilated area or fume hood. Clean up all spills immediately (lee2016particletechnologyand pages 4-7, lee2016particletechnologyand pages 1-4).

- **Wet sieving:** Eliminates airborne-dust and static risks but introduces solvent-flammability and Al–water reactivity hazards. Never use water with Al powder. IPA or ethanol are flammable; ventilation and spark-free environments are essential (kaya2026calculationsforhazardous pages 41-45, batistao2026surfacefunctionalizationof pages 85-90).

- **Air-jet sieve:** The integral vacuum system is a major concern. Standard vacuum cleaners have brush motors (sparking) and non-conductive plastic components. An Al-rated collection system with conductive grounded components is required. The fines fraction is concentrated in the vacuum stream (lee2016particletechnologyand pages 4-7).

- **Air classifier:** Must operate in inert gas (N₂ or Ar) at O₂ below LOC (~10%). Collection cyclone and filter must be ATEX-rated. Grounding of all components is mandatory (sezerUnknownyearalümi̇nyumtozpatlamalarinin pages 212-216, lee2016particletechnologyand pages 4-7).

- **General lab handling per NFPA 484 / NFPA 652:** Housekeeping to prevent dust accumulation > 1/32 in (0.8 mm); bonding and grounding of all conductive equipment and containers; no open ignition sources; local exhaust ventilation at dust-release points; conductive containers for powder storage and transfer; moisture control to avoid H₂ generation from water-reactive metals (lee2016particletechnologyand pages 4-7, lee2016particletechnologyand pages 1-4, kaya2026calculationsforhazardous pages 41-45).

## 10. Recommendation for a Lab Making 100–250 g per Run

### Primary Recommendation: Relax the Lower Cut to 20 µm and Use a Two-Stage Approach

Given the constraints (100–250 g per atomization run, no glovebox, 200 mm sieves, university budget), the most realistic approach is:

**Stage 1 — Upper cut with a mechanical sieve shaker (essential purchase):** Acquire a compact vibratory or tapping shaker for 200 mm sieves. Use the 63 µm and 45 µm sieves on the shaker with 100–200 g charges and 15–30 min cycles, per ISO 4497 / ASTM B 214 (neikov2019powdercharacterizationand pages 3-4). This reliably produces the upper cut at 45 or 63 µm. For 200–500 g lots, run 1–3 passes. This is the minimum necessary investment and addresses the question of whether a shaker is needed: **yes, unequivocally.**

**Stage 2 — Lower cut:** The 15–25 µm lower cut is the difficult part. Given the SEM evidence that the smallest particles from the rePOWDER are mostly 40–60 µm, the fraction below 20 µm is likely very small (<2–5% by volume, based on the nickel-aluminium bronze data provided). Therefore:

- **If the sub-20 µm fraction is negligible (<2% by volume as measured by laser diffraction):** A lower cut may not be necessary. Simply use the 45 µm or 63 µm upper sieve and accept the full fines content for initial LPBF trials. Measure the PSD by laser diffraction to confirm.

- **If a lower cut is required:** The most practical laboratory-scale option is a **32 µm woven-wire or micromesh sieve on the same shaker**, used with small charges (25–50 g), sieving aids (rubber balls, antistatic spray), and extended sieving times (20–30 min per pass). This will not produce a sharp 32 µm cut—the transition zone will span roughly 20–45 µm—but it will remove the majority of sub-25 µm fines. Expect throughput of approximately 50–150 g/h and losses of 2–5%.

- **For a true 15–20 µm cut:** This requires access to an **air classifier (Hosokawa Alpine 50 ATP or equivalent) operating under inert gas**. This is best arranged through collaboration with a university or research institute that has such equipment, rather than purchasing one (cost >€50,000, plus ATEX compliance). Alternatively, toll classification can be attempted if lots of 2–5 kg can be accumulated. The documented approach of Cui et al. (2023), who used an Alpine 50 ATP to remove <20 µm fines followed by 63 µm sieving (cui2023gasatomizationof pages 2-4), is the closest published workflow to what this lab needs.

### What Not to Do

- **Do not wet-sieve Al powder in water:** Hydrogen evolution and severe oxidation render the powder unsuitable for LPBF (batistao2026surfacefunctionalizationof pages 85-90).
- **Do not use a standard vacuum cleaner with an air-jet sieve for Al powder:** This is an explosion risk (lee2016particletechnologyand pages 4-7).
- **Do not rely on hand sieving at 45 µm:** It is unreproducible and standards-noncompliant for near-median cuts (neikov2019powdercharacterizationand pages 3-4).

### Practical Starting Point

For immediate use: purchase a sieve shaker (~$3,000–8,000), stack the 250 µm / 63 µm / 45 µm sieves, process the 100–250 g rePOWDER output in a single shaker cycle (15–20 min), collect the −45 µm fraction, and measure its PSD by laser diffraction. If the sub-20 µm content is <2–3%, proceed to LPBF trials with the 20–45 µm window. If further classification is needed, add a 25 or 32 µm sieve and reduce the charge per pass. Ground all equipment, work in a ventilated area, and follow NFPA 484 dust-handling precautions throughout.
